The reproductive biology of the Blue-eyed cockatoo (Cacatua ophthalmica) is characterized by a relatively slow pace of life, typical of many large-bodied parrots. Females produce a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = a single egg per clutch], a modest fecundity that is offset by extended parental care. Under the active metabolic body temperature of approximately 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], most reproductive and developmental events proceed. The species typically raises approximately one brood every two years [F_R_i = approximately one brood every two years], a rate constrained by the long chick dependence period. This low annual reproductive output is balanced by a notably extended lifespan. The maximum recorded longevity for the species in the wild reaches approximately fifty years [am = approximately fifty years], a duration that allows individuals multiple breeding opportunities over their lifetime at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This life-history strategy, centered on high adult survival and low per-event fecundity, is a hallmark of many island-endemic and large psittacines.

Hatchlings of the Blue-eyed cockatoo emerge from eggs incubated at a steady 36 °C [T = 36 °C], with the age at hatching recorded as 28 days [ab = 28 days] under those conditions. At birth, the wet weight of a neonate is approximately 20.7 grams [Wwb = approximately 20.7 grams], a modest mass consistent with the altricial development pattern of large parrots, where energy is prioritized for rapid growth under intensive parental care. This initial weight reflects the substantial yolk reserves that sustain the nestling through its first days of life. The species is altricial, meaning chicks are born blind, naked, and entirely dependent on parental provisioning for warmth and food. The incubation period, typical of cockatoos, is a critical phase during which the developing embryo relies on the consistent thermal environment provided by the attending parents. Any significant deviation from the optimal incubation temperature can prolong the developmental period or reduce hatchling viability, underscoring the importance of stable nest cavity microclimates for successful reproduction in this species.

As the nestling progresses through its developmental stages, it undergoes a remarkable transformation in body mass. Field studies have documented that the ultimate wet weight of a fully grown adult is approximately 560 grams [Wwi = approximately 560 grams], a size that reflects the species' robust build and strong flying capability. This represents a more than twenty-five-fold increase from the hatchling mass, a growth trajectory that is sustained by the diligent feeding efforts of both parents. During the nestling period, the chick is fed a diet of seeds, fruits, and occasionally insect larvae, all of which are gathered from the surrounding forest canopy. The parents engage in multiple feeding trips each day to meet the chick's escalating energy demands. This intensive provisioning continues until the young bird reaches a stage of development where it is capable of leaving the nest and attempting its first flights, a milestone that is a key step toward independence.

Under the typical active thermoregulatory conditions of the species at 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C], the time from hatching to fledging is approximately 120 days from hatching [tx = approximately 120 days from hatching]. This extended nestling period is one of the longest recorded among cockatoos and is associated with the slow development of flight feathers and the acquisition of foraging skills necessary for survival after nest departure. During this phase, the growing chick begins to exercise its wings within the nest cavity, strengthening the flight muscles in preparation for its first flight. The fledgling, upon leaving the nest, remains in close association with its parents for several additional weeks, during which it learns to identify food sources and avoid predators. This post-fledging dependence is a critical period of learning that significantly influences the young bird's chances of survival in the demanding environment of the lowland and hill forests it inhabits.

Sexual maturation in the Blue-eyed cockatoo is a gradual process, with individuals reaching puberty at approximately 360 days after hatching [tp = approximately 360 days after hatching] under the species' typical active body temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. However, the age at which breeding first occurs is typically deferred further, with the time since birth at first reproduction recorded as about 3 years since birth [tR = about 3 years since birth] at a temperature of 41.3 °C [T = 41.3 °C]. This delay between reaching physiological sexual maturity and initiating a first breeding attempt is common in long-lived parrots and is thought to be related to the time required for young birds to acquire a breeding territory, establish a pair bond, and develop the necessary foraging proficiency to successfully provision offspring. Males, in particular, may not secure a breeding position until they are approximately 5 years old, as competition for nest hollows and suitable mates is intense. This slow pace of reproductive maturation ensures that only experienced individuals with access to high-quality resources engage in the energetically costly process of reproduction.
